title: Ongoing, or done
goal: Adding the prefix و-, which separates an action in progress from a completed one — one letter that changes the meaning of the whole sentence, and moves the stress.
bekal: tell an ongoing action from a completed one
attach و- correctly, including on verbs that refuse it
move the stress onto و- so the meaning comes through

dialogs.title: خبرې اترې — یو لیست او یو بازار
dialogs.intro: Najib has to go to work and leaves Budi a few errands. A small piece of paper changes hands, and with it a grammar lesson.

lines.speaker: نجیب:
lines.text: بودي، یو کار لرم. دا لیست ولوله.
lines.baca: Būdī, yaw kār larəm. dā līst wə́lwala.
lines.id: Budi, I have a favor to ask. Read this list.
lines.literal: Budi, one job have-I. this list read-done.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.id: Read it all the way through? But I'm reading right now!

lines.speaker: نجیب:
lines.text: هو، خو ولوله یعنې تر پایه. لولې یعنې اوس.
lines.baca: ho, kho wə́lwala ya'nē tər pāya. lwale ya'nē os.
lines.id: Yes, but ولوله means to the end. لولې means now.
lines.literal: yes, but read-done means until end. read-you means now.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: نو یو حرف ټول معنی بدلوي؟
lines.baca: no yaw harf ṭol ma'nā badalawī?
lines.id: So one letter changes the whole meaning?
lines.literal: so one letter all meaning changes-it?

lines.speaker: نجیب:
lines.text: هو. او زور هم بدلېږي — و لومړی وي.
lines.baca: ho. aw zor ham badleẓī — wə lūmṛay wī.
lines.id: Yes. And the stress changes too — و comes first.
lines.literal: yes. and stress also changes — و first usually-is.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: ښه. په لیست کې څه دي؟
lines.baca: ṣa. pə līst ke tsə dī?
lines.literal: good. on list in what are?

lines.speaker: نجیب:
lines.text: ډوډۍ واخله، چای واخله، او دا لیک ولیکه.
lines.baca: ḍoḍəy wākhla, chāy wākhla, aw dā līk wə́lika.
lines.id: Buy bread, buy tea, and write this letter.
lines.literal: bread take-done, tea take-done, and this letter write-done.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.id: Who should I write the letter to?

lines.speaker: نجیب:
lines.text: زما ښوونکي ته. خو ژر یې ولیکه، زه ماسپښین ځم.
lines.baca: zmā ṣowunkī ta. kho zhər ye wə́lika, zə māspaṣīn dzəm.
lines.id: To my teacher. But write it quickly, I'm leaving this afternoon.
lines.literal: my teacher to. but quickly it write-done, I afternoon go-I.

lines.speaker: نجیب:
lines.text: هېڅکله وراځم مه وایه. راتلل خپل مخکینی برخه لري.
lines.baca: hetskəla wərādzəm ma wāya. rātləl khpəl məkhkinay barkha larī.

lines.text: نو د راتلل تېر بڼه څه ده؟
lines.baca: no də rātləl ter baṇa tsə da?

lines.speaker: نجیب:
lines.id: راغلم. There's no و in it at all.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: ښه، پوه شوم. زه اوس ځم او ډوډۍ اخلم.
lines.baca: ṣa, poh shwəm. zə os dzəm aw ḍoḍəy akhləm.
lines.id: OK, I get it. I'm going now and buying bread.
lines.literal: good, understanding became-I. I now go-I and bread take-I.

lines.text: نه — واخله! تر پایه، نه لږ لږ.
lines.baca: nə — wākhla! tər pāya, nə ləẓ ləẓ.

lines.literal: no — take-done! until end, not little little.

notes: Here is an idea English has no exact match for. Pashto doesn't care much about **when** something happens; what it always marks is whether the action is **complete or not**. The prefix و- is the marker of completion, and it goes in front of the verb.

⚠️ The stress moves with و-. لیکم is said *likə́m*, stressed at the end, while ولیکم is said *wə́likəm*, stressed on **و**. To an Afghan ear, the stress is what really tells them apart — not the letter on paper.

Compare these two sentences carefully. کتاب لولم means "I am reading a book" or "I read books"; کتاب ولولم means "so that I read the book to the end". The second one shows up mostly in commands, requests, and plans.

Some verbs **refuse** و-, for a simple reason: they already have a prefix of their own. راتلل (to come) already opens with را · کېناستل (to sit) opens with کې · پاڅېدل (to get up) opens with پا. For these verbs, the only sign of completion is the shift in stress.

For now you don't need to use و- perfectly. What matters is that you **recognize** it when you hear it, and know it isn't a slip of the tongue. Units 12 to 14 use it constantly, and it will stick on its own.

The phrase پوه شوم means "I understand", literally "understanding became-I". It's a past form, and Afghans use it exactly where an English speaker says "oh, I see" — right after the understanding arrives.

grammars.title: 🔴 The prefix و-: the mark of a completed action
body: The rule for attaching it is simple: و- goes in front of the verb, and the stress moves onto it. If the verb begins with long ا, the prefix becomes وا — so اخلم turns into **واخلم**.
⚠️ The prefix و- is not used for habits or for states still in progress. هره ورځ **ولیکم** is wrong; habits always take the plain form هره ورځ لیکم.

grammars.title: Where و- shows up in everyday sentences
body: These three places are the ones you'll meet most often, and in all three و- is almost always required. If you remember only one, make it the first: commands and requests.
Note that و- does not mean "past". It can appear in a command for tomorrow, in a plan for next week, and in a story about yesterday — what it marks is completion, not time.

sections.title: The eight most common verbs, both forms at once

blocks.text: The verbs below cover most of everyday conversation, and every one of them changes shape when و- is added. Learn the third column as new words, not as something you work out — it's the fastest way, and it's what Afghan children do.
Negating a completed sentence: نه goes in the middle
This is the one place where Pashto splits its verb. نه doesn't stand in front of the whole word; it slips **between** و- and the verb stem, and the stress stays on و-.

blocks.title: If you're still unsure about و-
items: Use the plain form. کتاب لولم is still understood perfectly; it just sounds like an action in progress, not a finished one.
What you must **not** do is put و- on a habit. هره ورځ ولولم sounds wrong, because a habit by its nature is never complete.
For commands, always use و-. A command without و- sounds like asking someone to keep doing it **over and over**, which is rarely what you mean.
Listen for the stress in everyday speech. Once your ear catches the difference between *likə́m* and *wə́likəm*, your mouth will follow without forcing it.

blocks.title: Phrases you need this week
items: Polite request: **لطفاً یو ځل بیا ووایئ** *lutfan yaw dzal byā wowāyəy* — "please say it once more".
Taking on a task: **ښه، اوس یې کوم** *ṣa, os ye kawəm* — "OK, I'll do it now".
Reporting it's done: **وشول** *wə́shwəl* — "all done". One word, and it's used constantly.
Saying you understand: **پوه شوم** *poh shwəm* — "I understand". Its partner: **پوه نه شوم** *poh nə shwəm*.

answers: ونه لیکه — ونه خله — ونه خوره — ونه وایه — ونه کړه

wave: Say these pairs out loud ten times today: *likə́m* then *wə́likəm*, *khorə́m* then *wə́khorəm*. What you're training isn't the letters but where the stress falls.
